quote: Trinity, which exceedeth all Being, Deity, and Goodness! Thou that instructeth Christians in Thy heavenly wisdom! Guide us to that topmost height of mystic lore which exceedeth light and more than exceedeth knowledge, where the simple, absolute, and unchangeable mysteries of heavenly Truth lie hidden in the dazzling obscurity of the secret Silence, outshining all brilliance with the intensity of their darkness, and surcharging our blinded intellects with the utterly impalpable and invisible fairness of glories which exceed all beauty! Such be my prayer; and thee, dear Timothy, I counsel that, in the earnest exercise of mystic contemplation, thou leave the senses and the activities of the intellect and all things that the senses or the intellect can perceive, and all things in this world of nothingness, or in that world of being, and that, thine understanding being laid to rest, thou strain (so far as thou mayest) towards an union with Him whom neither being nor understanding can contain.
author: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
work: Mystical Theology, ch. 1 (trans. C. E. Rolt, 1920)
expansion:
This is the hinge of the via negativa, the passage where the Mystical Theology starts its run of negations. The text you liked most recently, "Learn to listen to the secret Silence… Trinity, which exceedeth all Being," is the prayer that opens the same treatise. Dionysius takes the Neoplatonic logic of Proclus (the One gives what it does not itself have) and turns it into a discipline of speech about God. Whatever we affirm of creatures has to be denied of their cause, and the reason is not lack. The cause stands beyond the whole opposition of having and lacking. Jones's translation keeps the scholastic flavor with "in preeminence" (kath' hyperochēn). The negations are hyper-negations, not privations.

The structure matters. In the Divine Names, affirmative (kataphatic) theology comes down from the highest names (Good, Being, Life) toward the lowest. Apophatic theology climbs back up by stripping those names away. Chapters 4 and 5 deny first sensible and then intelligible predicates, and end by denying the denials themselves: the cause is "beyond every assertion and every denial." This is no license for vagueness. It is a very precise grammar of transcendence, and it explains how Eckhart could later speak of the "Godhead" beyond "God."

For your sensibility, the passage gives an exact account of why the rationalist's grasp is not the measure of truth (you liked "if you think of truth only in rationalistic terms, you have confused what you can grasp with what is true"). Dionysius doesn't oppose reason. He puts it inside a liturgical and contemplative ascent that ends in agnōsia, a knowing through unknowing. That ascent is the line running through the Cloud of Unknowing, John of the Cross, and the Orthodox hesychasts.

quote: Hierarchy is, in my opinion, a holy order and knowledge and activity which, so far as is attainable, participates in the Divine Likeness, and is lifted up to the illuminations given it from God, and correspondingly towards the imitation of God. Now the Beauty of God, being unific, good, and the Source of all perfection, is wholly free from dissimilarity, and bestows its own Light upon each according to his merit; and in the most divine Mysteries perfects them in accordance
author: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
work: The Celestial Hierarchy, ch. III.1 (trans. John Parker, 1894)
expansion:
Dionysius coined the word "hierarchy" (hierarchia, "sacred source" or "sacred rule"), and his definition has nothing to do with the bureaucratic ladder the word later came to mean. A hierarchy here is three things at once: an order (taxis), a knowledge (epistēmē), and an activity (energeia). Its whole purpose is assimilation to God and union with Him (aphomoiōsis te kai henōsis). Each rank receives the divine light and passes it on in the measure it can bear, through three movements: purification, illumination, perfection.

Two things set this apart from the hierarchy of power. First, the light is not owned by any rank. It goes through each one the way sunlight goes through layers of glass, so that the higher rank serves the lower by passing on what it received. Second, every member of the hierarchy is said to be a "fellow worker with God" (synergos theou), so that receiving is an action rather than a passive state. Later medieval cosmology, Dante's Paradiso and the Gothic theology of light associated with Abbot Suger all draw on this text.

This gives a concept that matches your interest in order and tradition without collapsing into politics. You liked Weininger's line that "the principle of all aristocracy is the precise observance of all boundaries between people," and Guénon's account of the elite. Dionysius's hierarchy is the theological original of those ideas, and it carries a demanding correction: rank is justified only as transmission, and it ends in deification rather than domination.

quote: Those who seek peace in external things, whether in places or devotional practices, people or works, in withdrawal from the world or poverty or self-abasement: however great these things may be or whatever their character, they are still nothing at all and cannot be the source of peace. Those who seek in this way, seek wrongly, and the farther they range, the less they find what they are looking for. They proceed like someone who has lost their way: the farther they go, the more lost they become. But what then should they do? First of all, they should renounce themselves, and then they will have renounced all things. Truly, if someone were to renounce a kingdom or the whole world while still holding on to themselves, then they would have renounced nothing at all. And indeed, if someone renounces themselves, then whatever they might keep, whether it be a kingdom or honour or whatever it may be, they will still have renounced all things. […] Examine yourself, and wherever you find yourself, then take leave of yourself. This is the best way of all.
author: Meister Eckhart
work: The Talks of Instruction (Reden der Unterweisung, c. 1294–98), §3 (trans. Oliver Davies, Selected Writings, Penguin 1994)
expansion:
The Talks of Instruction were given to Dominican novices in Erfurt around 1294–98. They are the earliest place where Eckhart develops what later German mysticism called Gelassenheit, "releasement" or "letting-be." The surrounding text attacks the idea that peace comes from places, devotional practices, withdrawal from the world, or even poverty: "Those who seek in this way, seek wrongly." The obstacle is never the outer situation. It is the self-will that brings itself into every situation.

"Take leave of yourself" (lâz dich) is the root of the verb lassen, from which Gelassenheit comes. It is not self-hatred and it is not quietism. The later sermons push it into the doctrine of Abgeschiedenheit (detachment) and of the "ground" (grunt) where "God's ground is my ground and my ground is God's ground." Releasement is the condition for the birth of the Word in the soul. Heidegger later took the word Gelassenheit for his 1955 Memorial Address on thinking that does not calculate, so the term reaches from Eckhart into the twentieth-century critique of technology.

This answers the question behind many of your likes about self-worth and not needing outside validation. The self-help version says to build a secure ego. Eckhart says the secure ego is still the problem. The freedom he means is freedom from oneself, which is why it can sit alongside humility rather than pride.

quote: The man who abides in the will of God wills nothing else than what God is, and what He wills. If he were ill he would not wish to be well. If he really abides in God's will, all pain is to him a joy, all complication, simple: yea, even the pains of hell would be a joy to him. He is free and gone out from himself, and from all that he receives, he must be free. If my eye is to discern colour, it must itself be free from all colour. The eye with which I see God is the same with which God sees me. My eye and God's eye is one eye, and one sight, and one knowledge, and one love.
author: Meister Eckhart
work: Sermon IV, "True Hearing" (trans. Claud Field)
expansion:
This is one of the propositions that made Eckhart's later trial at Avignon (1327–29) inevitable. It is also one of the most exact statements of his theory of knowledge. Just before this passage he argues that "if my eye is to discern colour, it must itself be free from all colour." Vision needs a receptive emptiness, the scholastic principle that the knower becomes the known in act, which Eckhart takes from Aristotle's De Anima through Aquinas and then pushes to its limit.

The claim is not that the soul is God by nature. Eckhart separates the created powers of the soul from an uncreated "something" (ein etwaz) in it, the "little castle" or "spark" (vünkelîn). In that ground knowing is no longer a subject looking at an object. It becomes one act shared by two. This is why he can say God's eye and mine are one sight: the vision is the act, and in the act there is no second.

Read next to Plotinus ("one must become godlike to see the god"), Goethe's delicate empiricism, and Corbin's imaginal, the line points to a theme that keeps returning in your likes: knowledge as participation rather than detached observation. It is the strongest premodern alternative to the Cartesian spectator.

quote: The sensitive eye can never be able to survey, the orb of the sun, unless strongly endued with solar fire, and participating largely of the vivid ray. Everyone therefore must become divine, and of godlike beauty, before he can gaze upon a god and the beautiful itself.
author: Plotinus
work: Enneads I.6 "On Beauty," §9 (trans. Thomas Taylor, 1787)
expansion:
This is the end of the first treatise Plotinus wrote, and the classic statement of the principle that like is known by like. Plato already called the eye the most "sunlike" (hēlioeidestaton) of the organs (Republic 508b). Plotinus makes that into a rule of spiritual method: you cannot see beauty from outside. You become able to see it only to the degree you are formed by it. Thomas Taylor's translation is the one Blake, Coleridge and Emerson read, which partly explains the Romantic afterlife of the text.

Ennead I.6 moves from bodily beauty to the beauty of virtues, then to Intellect (Nous), and finally to the Good, which is "beyond beauty" and its source. The famous instruction "never cease chiseling your statue" comes just before this passage. The ascent is ascetic and aesthetic at once: the soul purifies itself by cutting away what is not itself, the way a sculptor reveals a form.

This is close to the center of your 2026 likes, where beauty, the sacred and the inner life overlap: Shishkin's forests, Bach's "refreshment of the spirit," Dostoevsky's beauty. Plotinus says why beauty is not decoration. It is the visible sign of a likeness to the source, and seeing it changes the one who sees.

quote: This, therefore, is mathematics: she reminds you of the invisible form of the soul; she gives life to her own discoveries; she awakens the mind and purifies the intellect; she brings light to our intrinsic ideas; she abolishes oblivion and ignorance which are ours by birth.
author: Proclus
work: Commentary on the First Book of Euclid's Elements (as quoted in Morris Kline, Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times, 1972)
expansion:
Proclus (412–485), head of the Athenian Academy, is the great systematizer of late Neoplatonism, and Dionysius's main hidden source. For him mathematics is a middle realm between the indivisible Forms and divisible bodies, and its objects are projected by the soul from its own logoi (rational principles) onto the screen of the imagination. That is why mathematics "reminds" the soul: geometry is anamnesis, Plato's recollection, carried out under discipline.

The phrase "abolishes oblivion" is meant literally: lēthē (forgetting) is the soul's condition after its fall into generation, and the mathematical sciences are the first rung of its return. Kepler quoted this commentary at length in the Harmonices Mundi, which is one route from Proclus to modern science's founding sense that the cosmos is geometrical because it is mind-like.

This links up with your liking of Cicero's Dream of Scipio and the music of the spheres. Proclus is the philosopher of that intuition: number, harmony and beauty are one order seen through different faculties. It is also a counterweight to the modern idea that mathematics is merely instrumental.

quote: We men have one book in common which points to God. Each has it within himself, which is the priceless Name of God. Its letters are the flames of His love, which He out of His heart in the priceless Name of Jesus has revealed in us. Read these letters in your hearts and spirits and you have books enough. All the writings of the children of God direct you unto that one book, for therein lie all the treasures of wisdom. … This book is Christ in you.
author: Jakob Böhme
work: Libri Apologetici, Book I (as quoted in the Wikiquote collection)
expansion:
Böhme (1575–1624) was a shoemaker in Görlitz. He had a vision while looking at sunlight reflected in a pewter dish, and he became the source of most later German theosophy, Romantic Naturphilosophie, and much of Hegel and Schelling. The local pastor condemned his books, and Böhme answered him with these apologetic writings. The "book within" is his answer to a scriptural literalism that he thought had turned the Word into dead letters.

His theology is unusually dynamic. God emerges from an Ungrund, a groundless abyss, through a dialectic of desire, darkness and light, the "seven source-spirits" (Quellgeister). Nature is the self-revelation of that process, so the book of nature and the book of the heart are the same text. Blake, whom you call one of your favorite Christian mystics, read Böhme in the William Law edition and said Paracelsus and Behmen had shown him things Swedenborg missed.

Böhme stands where several of your interests meet: Christian mysticism (Eckhart, Dionysius), the Romantic philosophy of nature (Goethe, Novalis, Schelling), and Jung's psychology of opposites. Jung's alchemical studies take Böhme seriously; the mandala essays in Collected Works 9i belong to that symbolic world, but they are not an essay on Böhme. If you want to read one writer who unites mysticism, alchemy and dialectic, start here.

quote: Someday someone will write a pathology of experimental physics and bring to light all those swindles which subvert our reason, beguile our judgment and, what is worse, stand in the way of any practical progress. The phenomena must be freed once and for all from their grim torture chamber of empiricism, mechanism, and dogmatism; they must be brought before the jury of man’s common sense. […] Nature will reveal nothing under torture; its frank answer to an honest question is “Yes! Yes!—No! No!” More than this comes of evil. […] There is a delicate empiricism which makes itself utterly identical with the object, thereby becoming true theory. But this enhancement of our mental powers belongs to a highly evolved age.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
work: Maxims and Reflections, nos. 430–431 and 509 (trans. in Goethe, Scientific Studies, ed. & trans. Douglas Miller, 1988, p. 307)
expansion:
"Es gibt eine zarte Empirie, die sich mit dem Gegenstand innigst identisch macht und dadurch zur eigentlichen Theorie wird." This maxim is the methodological core of Goethe's science: the Metamorphosis of Plants (1790), the Theory of Colours (1810), and his morphology. It goes with a companion maxim: "Let us not seek for something beyond the phenomena: they themselves are the theory." Theory (theōria) gets back its Greek meaning of contemplative seeing, as opposed to a hypothetical model standing behind appearances.

Goethe's opponent is the experimental method of Newton, which he accused of putting phenomena on the rack and forcing nature to answer under torture. Delicate empiricism asks for exact, patient, repeated observation of a phenomenon in all its variations, and then "exact sensorial imagination" (exakte sinnliche Phantasie) that lets the series of forms come together into an intuition of the living law, the Urphänomen. A related saying: "every object, well contemplated, opens a new organ of perception in us."

For you this is the bridge between Romanticism and an epistemology you can actually practice. It anticipates phenomenology, Steiner's and Henri Bortoft's "Goethean science," and McGilchrist's right-hemisphere mode of attention. Goethe's own warning matters too: the method "belongs to a highly evolved age." It demands a cultivation of perception, Bildung of the senses, which modernity has not done.

quote: Theories usually result from the precipitate reasoning of an impatient mind which would like to be rid of phenomena and replaces them with images, concepts, indeed often with mere words. […] Truth is contrary to our nature, not so error, and this for a very simple reason; truth demands that we should recognize ourselves as limited, error flatters us that, in one way or another, we are unlimited. […] Scientific knowledge helps us mainly because it makes the wonder to which we are called by nature rather more intelligible.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
work: Maxims and Reflections, nos. 428, 310 and 417 (trans. Elisabeth Stopp, Penguin 1998)
expansion:
This is the polemical side of delicate empiricism. Goethe's charge is psychological as well as logical: the impatient mind can't stand the openness of the phenomenon and wants it settled, turned into a manageable sign. The theory replaces the thing, and the word replaces the theory. The language anticipates Bergson's critique of the intellect's "cinematographic" habit and Heidegger's critique of representation (Vorstellung).

Goethe is not against theory. His complaint is about premature theory, which he elsewhere calls a "hasty attempt to get rid of the phenomena." The remedy is a moral discipline, renunciation (Entsagung). Wilhelm Meisters Wanderjahre is subtitled Die Entsagenden, "The Renunciants," and in the study of nature the same habit means holding back from conclusions until the phenomenon has fully shown itself.

The maxim matches Keats's Negative Capability ("without any irritable reaching after fact and reason"), which you liked, and Gómez Dávila's observation that "confused ideas and muddy ponds appear deep." Read together they describe an ethics of attention common to the Romantic and conservative critiques of modern rationalism.

quote: Everywhere we seek the Absolute, and always we find only things. […] Denotation by means of sounds and markings is a remarkable abstraction. Three letters designate God for me; several lines a million things. How easy becomes the manipulation of the universe here, how evident the concentration of the intellectual world! Language is the dynamics of the spiritual realm. One word of command moves armies; the word Liberty entire nations.
author: Novalis (Friedrich von Hardenberg)
work: Pollen (Blüthenstaub, 1798), Fragments 1–2 (English as given in the Wikiquote collection)
expansion:
The German is a pun that can't be translated: "Wir suchen überall das Unbedingte, und finden immer nur Dinge." Das Unbedingte, "the unconditioned," literally means the un-thinged. So the sentence says the Absolute is by definition what can never appear as a thing (Ding). It opens Pollen, the fragment collection Novalis published in the Schlegels' Athenaeum, and it sums up the early Romantic answer to Fichte: the ground of consciousness can't be caught by reflection, only intimated.

Philosophers now read early German Romanticism (Frühromantik) as a serious epistemology rather than a mood. Manfred Frank and Frederick Beiser have shown that Novalis and Friedrich Schlegel argued that philosophy's search for a first principle is an endless approximation. That is why the fragment, the irony, and the poetic "romanticizing" of the world are its proper forms. "To romanticize," Novalis wrote, "is to give the common a higher meaning, the ordinary a mysterious appearance."

For you, this states the dilemma you return to: the Absolute is wanted and never possessed. It also recasts apophatic theology in a post-Kantian key. Novalis is the bridge between Dionysius's "beyond being" and the modern self-conscious mind.

quote: Imagination places the future world for us either above or below or in reincarnation. We dream of travels throughout the universe: is not the universe within us? We do not know the depths of our spirit. The mysterious path leads within. In us, or nowhere, lies eternity with its worlds, the past and the future. […] Self-alienation is the source of all degradation as well as, on the contrary, the basis of all true elevation. The first step will be a look inward, an isolating contemplation of our self. Whoever remains standing here proceeds only halfway. The second step must be an active look outward, an autonomous, determined observation of the outer world.
author: Novalis (Friedrich von Hardenberg)
work: Pollen (Blüthenstaub, 1798), Fragments 16 and 24
expansion:
"Nach innen geht der geheimnisvolle Weg" (inward goes the mysterious path) became a slogan of German Romanticism. It is not a recommendation of introspective subjectivism. Fragment 24 is not the next fragment: 17 through 23 stand between it and fragment 16. It insists that the first step is a look inward, but that whoever stops there "proceeds only halfway." The second step has to be an active look outward. The German word is Selbstentäußerung, a self-emptying or self-divestment, closer to kenosis than to the modern "self-alienation" of the English wording above. The inner path is a passage, not a retreat.

Novalis studied mining at the Freiberg Bergakademie under the geologist Werner. His inward journey is modelled on the miner's descent, a theme of Heinrich von Ofterdingen, where the old miner reads the earth like a book of history. The interior is cosmic: the universe in us is not a private mental space but the depth where self and nature are one, which is the Romantic form of the Hermetic microcosm.

This anticipates Jung's collective unconscious more exactly than almost any other pre-psychological text. You liked Robert A. Johnson's complaint that modern Westerners "try to get by without acknowledging inner life at all." Novalis is the source text for the opposite position.

quote: We are nothing; what we search for is everything. […] What is all that men have done and thought over thousands of years, compared with one moment of love. But in all Nature, too, it is what is nearest to perfection, what is most divinely beautiful! There all stairs lead from the threshold of life. From there we come, to there we go.
author: Friedrich Hölderlin
work: Fragment of Hyperion (Neue Thalia, 1793) and Hyperion, or the Hermit in Greece (1797–99)
expansion:
"Wir sind nichts; was wir suchen, ist alles." This is the earliest published version of Hölderlin's novel Hyperion, which Schiller printed in his journal. Its protagonist moves between the "eccentric path" of a fractured modern consciousness and the longing for lost unity with nature that he identifies with ancient Greece. The sentence states the whole tension: the self is empty, but it is constituted by a striving toward the All.

In the 1790s Hölderlin shared a room at the Tübingen seminary with Hegel and Schelling, and a short text likely written by him or with him, the "Oldest System-Program of German Idealism," calls for a "mythology of reason." Unlike his roommates, Hölderlin did not believe that reflection could recover the unity it had broken. In his fragment "Judgment and Being" (Urtheil und Seyn, 1795) he argues that Being is prior to the subject-object split and can't be reached by self-consciousness, only by beauty and poetry.

This pairs naturally with Novalis's "we seek the Absolute… and find only things," and it gives an exact philosophical form to the mood of many of your likes: melancholy that isn't nihilism, because the void is shaped by what it longs for. It is also the Romantic secular echo of Augustine's restless heart.

quote: Nah ist / Und schwer zu fassen der Gott. / Wo aber Gefahr ist, wächst / Das Rettende auch. [Literal English: Near is / And difficult to grasp, the God. / But where danger is, grows / The saving power also.]
author: Friedrich Hölderlin
work: "Patmos" (1803), lines 1–4; German text as in Gedichte von Friedrich Hölderlin (Reclam, Leipzig 1873), p. 133; English is a literal rendering
expansion:
The poem was dedicated to the Landgrave of Homburg and moves through John's exile on Patmos, the death of Christ, and the withdrawal of the gods. Its opening reads: "Near is / And difficult to grasp, the God. / But where danger is, grows / The saving power also." The lines are about theological presence and absence before they are about rescue. The god is near exactly because he is hard to grasp.

Heidegger made the lines famous in "The Question Concerning Technology" (1954). There he argues that the supreme danger of technology's essence, Gestell or enframing, which reveals everything as "standing-reserve," is also where a saving relation can grow, if we are able to experience the danger as danger. The saving power isn't a technical fix. It is a transformed way of seeing that Heidegger links to poiēsis and art.

Many of your likes worry about the age as a whole: the panopticon, hyper-optimization, AI, decline. Hölderlin and Heidegger offer the hard alternative to despair and to naive optimism alike. The way through is in the depth of the danger itself, which recalls Jung's insistence that the cure comes through the wound.

quote: The fear of speculation, the ostensible rush from the theoretical to the practical, brings about the same shallowness in action that it does in knowledge. It is by studying a strictly theoretical philosophy that we become most acquainted with Ideas, and only Ideas provide action with vigour and ethical meaning. […] All rules for study are summed up in this one: learn only in order to create.
author: F. W. J. Schelling
work: Lectures on the Method of Academic Study (Vorlesungen über die Methode des akademischen Studiums, 1803), Lecture 7 and Lecture 1 (English as given in Wikiquote)
expansion:
Schelling gave these fourteen lectures at Jena when he was twenty-seven. They are a manifesto for the university as an organic whole whose members (philosophy, theology, law, medicine, natural science, art) express one Absolute. The line "Lerne nur, um selbst zu schaffen" criticizes the "bread-and-butter" scholar who learns only to apply, and the pedant who learns only to store.

For Schelling creation is not self-expression. It is the human repetition of what nature does. In the System of Transcendental Idealism (1800) he argued that art, more than philosophy, is the "organon" of philosophy, because in the work of genius conscious and unconscious production coincide and the identity of spirit and nature becomes visible. To learn in order to create is to take part in that productive ground.

You liked the tweet complaining that "bookheads… bind themselves to a specialty." Schelling is the classic philosophical argument against that: knowledge cut off from the whole and from production goes dead. His later "positive philosophy" also connects to your interest in myth (his Philosophy of Mythology influenced Eliade and Jung).

quote: It therefore pauses at this particular thing; the course of time stops; the relations vanish for it; only the essential, the Idea, is its object. We may, therefore, accurately define it as the way of viewing things independent of the principle of sufficient reason, in opposition to the way of viewing them which proceeds in accordance with that principle, and which is the method of experience and of science. This last method of considering things may be compared to a line infinitely extended in a horizontal direction, and the former to a vertical line which cuts it at any point. The method of viewing things which proceeds in accordance with the principle of sufficient reason is the rational method, and it alone is valid and of use in practical life and in science. The method which looks away from the content of this principle is the method of genius, which is only valid and of use in art. The first is the method of Aristotle; the second is, on the whole, that of Plato.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
work: The World as Will and Idea, vol. I, Book III, §36 (trans. R. B. Haldane & J. Kemp, 1883)
expansion:
Book III of Schopenhauer's main work is a metaphysics of aesthetic contemplation. All ordinary cognition runs along the principle of sufficient reason: it asks why, where, when, and for what. It serves the will, so it is interested. In aesthetic contemplation the subject "loses himself" in the object and becomes "pure, will-less, painless, timeless subject of knowledge," and the object stops being a particular thing and becomes a Platonic Idea.

Genius, on this view, is not an unusually strong intellect. It is a surplus of intellect over will, which lets a person keep up the will-less gaze. That explains your earlier liked quote that "the intellect is not an extensive quantity, but an intensive one": genius is a different mode of seeing, not a larger amount of the ordinary one. Here Schopenhauer explicitly combines Plato and Kant.

This connects your Schopenhauer likes (all from 2026) with Goethe's zarte Empirie and Eckhart's releasement. All three describe a knowing that starts only when self-interest is set aside. It also explains why beauty works on you as relief: it is a temporary release from the will.

quote: Music is as direct an objectification and copy of the whole will as the world itself, nay, even as the Ideas, whose multiplied manifestation constitutes the world of individual things. Music is thus by no means like the other arts, the copy of the Ideas, but the copy of the will itself, whose objectivity the Ideas are. This is why the effect of music is so much more powerful and penetrating than that of the other arts, for they speak only of shadows, but it speaks of the thing itself.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
work: The World as Will and Idea, vol. I, Book III, §52 (trans. R. B. Haldane & J. Kemp, 1883)
expansion:
Schopenhauer gives music a unique metaphysical rank. The other arts copy the Ideas, the will's adequate objectifications. Music skips the Ideas and copies the will itself. Music "could still exist even if there were no world at all." Bass, harmony and melody correspond to the grades of nature from inorganic matter to human striving, and a melody's endless departure from and return to the tonic is the very form of desire.

This passage did more than any other philosophical text to shape the nineteenth-century cult of music. Wagner read it in 1854 and rebuilt Tristan und Isolde around it. Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy (1872) depends on it, and so in a way does his "without music, life would be a mistake."

Your likes include Bach's "glory of God and refreshment of the spirit," Glenn Gould on solitude, Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody, Cicero's music of the spheres, and a quote that "everything that… cannot be understood in relation to music engenders… disgust." Schopenhauer gives you the most radical metaphysics of that intuition. The Pythagorean-Christian tradition (Boethius, Kepler) makes a natural counterpoint: it hears in music the order of the cosmos rather than the will's restless striving.

quote: The archetype as such is a psychoid factor that belongs, as it were, to the invisible, ultraviolet end of the psychic spectrum. … It seems to me probable that the real nature of the archetype is not capable of being made conscious, that it is transcendent, on which account I call it psychoid. […] Just as the “psychic infra-red,” the biological instinctual psyche, gradually passes over into the physiology of the organism … so the “psychic ultra-violet,” the archetype, describes a field which exhibits none of the peculiarities of the physiological and yet, in the last analysis, can no longer be regarded as psychic.
author: C. G. Jung
work: "On the Nature of the Psyche" (1947/1954), Collected Works vol. 8 (trans. R. F. C. Hull), §§417, 420
expansion:
This essay is Jung's most rigorous theoretical work, and §417 is where he separates the archetype as such (an irrepresentable ordering factor) from archetypal images (the symbols in which it appears). He borrowed the word "psychoid" from the vitalist Hans Driesch and from Bleuler. The archetype is quasi-psychic. Like the infrared end of the spectrum, which shades into instinct and physiology, the archetype at the "ultraviolet" end shades into something that "can no longer be regarded as psychic."

The point is metaphysical. If the archetype is psychoid, the deepest layer of the unconscious is neither simply mental nor simply material. Jung concluded that psyche and matter may be "two different aspects of one and the same thing," and this is the theoretical basis for his work with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli on synchronicity (1952) and for the alchemical idea of the unus mundus that you have been reading about in Mysterium Coniunctionis.

This is the concept that keeps Jung from being reduced to self-help psychology. In Kantian terms it makes the archetype a limit-concept, close to the thing-in-itself, and it puts Jung next to the Neoplatonists and Corbin rather than next to clinical psychology. It is also why he can say God-images are psychological facts without claiming to settle the reality of God.

quote: To be sure, the more we are accustomed to them the more has constant usage polished them smooth, so that what remains of them is banal superficiality, clothed in almost senseless paradoxes. The mystery of the virgin birth, or the oneness of the Son with the Father, or the Trinity which is no triad, no longer lends wings to any philosophical fantasy. They have become mere objects of belief. It is not surprising that the religious need, the believing mind, and the philosophical speculation of the cultured European feel themselves attracted to the symbols of the ~East—the grandiose conceptions of divinity in India and the abysms of Taoistic philosophy in China—just as once before the heart and mind of the Greco-Roman were gripped by Christian ideas. There are many Europeans who surrendered so completely to the influence of the Christian symbol that they were enmeshed in the neurosis of a Kierkegaard; and others, again, whose relation to God, owing to a progressive impoverishment of symbolism, developed into an unbearably refined I-you relation. It is not surprising that such persons later succumbed to the magic of the fresh strangeness of Eastern symbols. This surrender is no defeat, but rather bears witness to the receptiveness and vitality of the religious sense.
author: C. G. Jung
work: "Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious" (1934), in The Integration of the Personality (trans. Stanley Dell, 1939), pp. 57–58
expansion:
This sentence contains Jung's whole diagnosis of modernity. The Reformation, then the Enlightenment, stripped away the symbolic and dogmatic forms (sacraments, saints, the Virgin, the rituals of the year) that held and mediated the archetypes. Jung's image for this is "the iconoclasm of the Reformation… made a breach in the protective wall of sacred images." Once the forms were gone, the powers they contained did not disappear. They went inward and became symptoms, or went outward and became ideologies.

That's why Jung thought it was no accident that psychology arose when it did. It is a stopgap discipline for a civilization that has lost its symbols. Calling the gods "archetypes" is not, for him, a reduction. It acknowledges that we have been driven to meet them in the only place we have left: dreams, neuroses, and the mass movements of the twentieth century, which he analyzed in "Wotan" (1936).

Your likes include Guénon, Spengler, Fulton Sheen on anxiety, and tweets against "hedonic nihilism." Jung gives the psychological mechanism behind those cultural critiques. It also explains why he valued tradition while not accepting a simple return to it: the symbols have to be re-experienced, not just restored.

quote: We are living in what the Greeks called the right time for a "metamorphosis of the gods," i.e. of the fundamental principles and symbols. This peculiarity of our time, which is certainly not of our conscious choosing, is the expression of the unconscious man within us who is changing. Coming generations will have to take account of this momentous transformation if humanity is not to destroy itself through the might of its own technology and science.
author: C. G. Jung
work: The Undiscovered Self (Gegenwart und Zukunft, 1957), ch. 7
expansion:
Jung wrote this late essay during the Cold War and the hydrogen bomb. It argues that the mass state, whether communist or liberal-technocratic, dissolves the individual into statistics, and that the only counterweight is the individual who has met his own unconscious. The "metamorphosis of the gods" is the shift of the Platonic month from Pisces to Aquarius, which Jung explored in Aion (1951). It is the transformation of the dominant symbolic order of a civilization.

The sentence continues: "Coming generations will have to take account of this momentous transformation if humanity is not to destroy itself through the might of its own technology and science." For Jung, technological power without symbolic transformation is a catastrophe. Collective religion can't carry out that transformation alone. It has to happen in individuals, "in the smallest of all things, the individual psyche."

This links three of your preoccupations: critique of mass society and media (Orwell, Tocqueville, Jünger), religious renewal (Sheen, Lewis), and inner work (Jung on intuitive introverts, acceptance). Jung's thesis is that these are one problem.

quote: We observe immediately that we are no longer reduced to the dilemma of thought and extension, to the schema of a cosmology and a gnoseology limited to the empirical world and the world of abstract understanding. Between the two is placed an intermediate world, which our authors designate as ‘alam al-mithal, the world of the Image, mundus imaginalis : a world as ontologically real as the world of the senses and the world of the intellect, a world that requires a faculty of perception belonging to it, a faculty that is a cognitive function, a noetic value, as fully real as the faculties of sensory perception or intellectual intuition. This faculty is the imaginative power, the one we must avoid confusing with the imagination that modern man identifies with “fantasy” and that, according to him, produces only the “imaginary.”
author: Henry Corbin
work: "Mundus Imaginalis, or the Imaginary and the Imaginal" (1964), in Swedenborg and Esoteric Islam (trans. L. Fox, 1995), p. 9
expansion:
Corbin (1903–1978) was Heidegger's first French translator and later the great Western interpreter of Persian Sufism and Shi'ite theosophy (Suhrawardī, Ibn ʿArabī, Mullā Sadrā). He coined "imaginal" to rescue a concept that modern French and English had lost: the ʿālam al-mithāl, a world of autonomous images, "the eighth climate," a place that is "no-where" (Nā-kojā-ābād).

The modern Western cosmos has two tiers, matter and abstract thought. That leaves imagination with nothing to do but produce the unreal. The traditional cosmology Corbin recovers has three tiers. Between sense and intellect there is a world of subtle bodies and real images, and the active imagination perceives it the way the eye perceives colors. That world is where visions, prophetic revelation, the resurrection body and the meaning of symbols have their ontological place.

This is the missing piece connecting your liked authors: Blake's "Imagination is the real and eternal world," Swedenborg, Jung's active imagination, Hillman's archetypal psychology (built on Corbin), and Goethe's exakte sinnliche Phantasie. Corbin even quotes the Cambridge Platonist Henry More's spissitudo spiritualis. If you only read one essay from this list, this might be the one.

quote: Decreation: to make something created pass into the uncreated. Destruction: to make something created pass into nothingness. A blameworthy substitute for decreation. Creation is an act of love and it is perpetual. At each moment our existence is God’s love for us. But God can only love himself. His love for us is love for himself through us. Thus, he who gives us our being loves in us the acceptance of not being. Our existence is made up only of his waiting for our acceptance not to exist. He is perpetually begging from us that existence which he gives. He gives it to us in order to beg it from us. Relentless necessity, wretchedness, distress, the crushing burden of poverty and of labour which wears us out, cruelty, torture, violent death, constraint, disease—all these constitute divine love. It is God who in love withdraws from us so that we can love him. For if we were exposed to the direct radiance of his love, without the protection of space, of time and of matter, we should be evaporated like water in the sun; there would not be enough ‘I’ in us to make it possible to surrender the ‘I’ for love’s sake.
author: Simone Weil
work: Gravity and Grace (La Pesanteur et la grâce, 1947), "Decreation" (trans. Emma Crawford & Mario von der Ruhr, Routledge 2002), pp. 32–33
expansion:
Gravity and Grace is Gustave Thibon's arrangement of Weil's notebooks. "Decreation" is her most demanding concept. She starts from the kabbalistic and kenotic idea that creation is God's withdrawal: "God consented through love to cease to be everything so that we might be something." Decreation is the creature's answering consent to stop being a separate "I" so that God can again be all. Destruction is its counterfeit, the ego annihilating itself or others, which is still the ego at work.

The concept is precise. What is undone is not the person's existence but its usurpation: "We possess nothing in the world… except the power to say 'I.' That is what we should give to God." Weil connects it to attention, which she calls the faculty that empties itself in order to receive, and to her analysis of affliction (malheur) as the place where necessity, the "screen" between God and us, is fully exposed.

This is the strongest modern counterpart of Eckhart's "take leave of yourself," and it is the harder side of the attention-based spirituality you liked ("Attention consists of suspending our thought, leaving it detached, empty"). Like Eckhart, Weil has been read both as a Christian mystic and as a Platonist. She called Plato "the father of Western mysticism."

quote: The needs of the soul can for the most part be listed in pairs of opposites which balance and complete one another. The human soul has need of equality and of hierarchy. Equality is the public recognition, effectively expressed in institutions and manners, of the principle that an equal degree of attention is due to the needs of all human beings. Hierarchy is the scale of responsibilities.
author: Simone Weil
work: The Need for Roots (L'Enracinement, 1949), Part I, "The Needs of the Soul"
expansion:
The Free French in London commissioned The Need for Roots in 1943 as a report on how France might be rebuilt after the war. Weil wrote it in the last months of her life. It begins with a remarkable claim: obligations come before rights, and a society has to be judged by whether it meets the soul's needs (order, liberty, obedience, responsibility, equality, hierarchy, honor, punishment, freedom of opinion, security and risk, private and collective property, truth), not just the body's.

The pairing is the method. Equality alone gives the leveling Tocqueville feared. Hierarchy alone gives domination. Weil's definitions keep them from contradicting each other: equality is "the public recognition… that an equal degree of attention is due to the needs of all human beings" and hierarchy is "the scale of responsibilities." Rootedness, she says, "is perhaps the most important and least recognized need of the human soul." You liked that sentence in 2026.

The book matters to your profile because it gives a traditionalist-sounding politics (roots, hierarchy, the sacredness of labor) rooted in compassion and attention rather than resentment. It is the best antidote to the purely reactive politics of your 2020 likes. T. S. Eliot wrote the preface to the English edition.

quote: Attention consists of suspending our thought, leaving it detached, empty, and ready to be penetrated by the object; it means holding in our minds, within reach of this thought, but on a lower level and not in contact with it, the diverse knowledge we have acquired which we are forced to make use of.
author: Simone Weil
work: "Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God," in Waiting for God (Attente de Dieu, 1950; trans. Emma Craufurd)
expansion:
The passage here is from "Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God" (1942), collected in Waiting for God. Weil's claim is that the real purpose of schoolwork is to train attention, the same faculty prayer uses. Attention, as she defines it in this essay, is negative: suspending thought, leaving it detached, empty, and ready to be penetrated by the object. It is the opposite of willpower. In her French it sits next to attente, waiting.

Two famous sentences are often folded into this one, and they are different texts. In a letter of 13 April 1942 to the poet Joë Bousquet, paralyzed by a war wound since 1918, she wrote "L'attention est la forme la plus rare et la plus pure de la générosité." In the 1943 essay on the human person she names the question this attention makes possible: "What are you going through?" Generosity, for her, is giving the other person a reality that cannot be faked. The school-studies passage is the method. Those two lines are what the method is for.

It belongs near the front of your reading because your recent likes quote Weil on attention almost word for word, and because Iris Murdoch built The Sovereignty of Good on this idea. Murdoch is a natural next step.

quote: Of course in the present day […] the world of work begins to become — threatens to become — our only world, to the exclusion of all else. The demands of the working world grow ever more total, grasping ever more completely the whole of human existence. […] It could even be said, perhaps, that this very opposition, this threat from the world of total work, is what characterizes the situation of philosophy today more than its own particular content. Philosophy increasingly adopts — necessarily, it seems — the character of the alien, of mere intellectual luxury, of that which seems ever more intolerable and unjustifiable, the more exclusively the demands of the daily world of work take over the world of man.
author: Josef Pieper
work: Leisure, the Basis of Culture (Musse und Kult, 1948), Part II, "The Philosophical Act" (trans. G. Malsbary, pp. 64–65)
expansion:
Pieper wrote this in 1947, in the rubble of postwar Germany, when everyone was talking about reconstruction and the work ethic. His provocation was to say that a civilization is founded on leisure (scholē, the root of "school"), not on work. Leisure is not idleness or a break to recover for more work. It is a receptive attitude of the soul that lets reality be seen and celebrated.

"Total work" (totale Arbeit) is his name for the world in which everything has to justify itself by its function, even the intellect, which becomes "intellectual work." Pieper goes back to the medieval distinction between ratio (discursive, laborious reasoning) and intellectus (simple, receptive intuition, "the effortless awareness"). The modern world honors only ratio. His Thomist claim is that the highest knowing is a gift received, not a product made.

This expands the critique of hyper-optimization you liked ("Hyper-optimization selects against weirdness") into a full anthropology, and it ties to Picard on the "holy uselessness" of silence and to Han's achievement society. It also explains what festival, worship and art are for, which a contemplative life needs.

quote: If someone needs the "unusual" to be moved to astonishment, that person has lost the ability to respond rightly to the wondrous, the mirandum, of being. The hunger for the sensational, posing, as it may, in "bohemian garb," is an unmistakable sign of the loss of the true power of wonder, for a bourgeois-ized humanity. […] It should now be clear that "wonder" and philosophizing are connected with each other in a more essential sense than may at first appear in the statement, "Philosophy begins in wonder." For wonder is not merely the beginning, in the sense of initium, the first stage or phase of philosophy. Rather, wonder is the beginning in the sense of the "principle" (principium), the abiding, ever-intrinsic origin of philosophizing. It is not true to say that the philosopher, insofar as he philosophizes, ever "emerges from his wonder" — if he does depart from his state of wonder, he has ceased to philosophize.
author: Josef Pieper
work: Leisure, the Basis of Culture, Part II, "The Philosophical Act" (trans. G. Malsbary, pp. 105–106)
expansion:
Pieper is commenting on the most famous founding sentences in Western philosophy: Plato's "wonder (thaumazein) is the feeling of the philosopher" (Theaetetus 155d) and Aristotle's "it is owing to their wonder that men both now begin and at first began to philosophize" (Metaphysics 982b). The common reading takes wonder as a starting push that knowledge then leaves behind. Pieper reverses that: whoever stops wondering has stopped philosophizing.

The argument rests on the in-between status of the philosopher. In the Symposium Diotima says that no god philosophizes, because the gods already know, and that fools don't either, because they think they already know. The philosopher lives in the metaxy, the in-between. Pieper adds that "if someone needs the 'unusual' to be moved to astonishment, that person has lost the ability to respond rightly to the wondrous… of being," which describes our appetite for sensation exactly.

This passage gives a grounded account of your liking for Keats's Negative Capability, Chesterton's "the world will never starve for want of wonders," and the tweet that "doubt is the crown of life." It also puts the contemplative attitude inside classical philosophy rather than against it.

quote: Silence is the only phenomenon today that is ‘useless’. It does not fit into the world of profit and utility; it simply is. It seems to have no other purpose; it cannot be exploited. […] Yet there is more help and healing in silence than in all the ‘useful things’. Purposeless, unexploitable silence suddenly appears at the side of the all-too-purposeful, and frightens us by its very purposelessness. It interferes with the regular flow of the purposeful. It strengthens the untouchable, it lessens the damage inflicted by exploitation. It makes things whole again, by taking them back from the world of dissipation into the world of wholeness. It gives things something of its own holy uselessness, for that is what silence itself is: holy uselessness.
author: Max Picard
work: The World of Silence (Die Welt des Schweigens, 1948; trans. Stanley Godman, 1952), p. 18
expansion:
Picard (1888–1965) was a Swiss doctor who left medicine for philosophical writing. Born Jewish, he converted to Catholicism. He met Rilke in Munich in 1918 and the friendship lasted. Gabriel Marcel, also a friend, wrote the preface to The World of Silence. A debt to T. S. Eliot is not documented. The World of Silence argues that silence is not the absence of speech but "a positive, a complete world in itself," older than language, the ground from which the word comes and to which it returns.

His diagnosis of modern language follows: when speech is cut off from silence it becomes "noise of words," an "orphaned tongue" that talks automatically. Picard was writing about radio, but his account of a "world without forgetting" and without forgiveness, where every word is present somewhere and can always come back, reads like a description of social media. Hitler in uns selbst (1946), two years before the German World of Silence (1948), traced fascism to the same fragmentation of the soul.

Your most recent like is Pseudo-Dionysius's "secret Silence." Picard is the modern phenomenologist of that silence, the Catholic counterpart to Heidegger on technology, and he explains why your likes keep coming back to solitude, Glenn Gould, and nature.

quote: It must be recognized that man in his limited and relative earthly life is capable of bringing about the beautiful and the valuable only when he believes in another life, unlimited, absolute, eternal. That is a law of his being. A contact with this mortal life exclusive of any other ends in the wearing-away of effective energy and a self-satisfaction that makes one useless and superficial. Only the spiritual man, striking his roots deep in infinite and eternal life, can be a true creator. But Humanism denied the spiritual man, handed over the eternal to the temporal, and took its stand by the natural man within the limited confines of the earth.
author: Nikolai Berdyaev
work: The End of Our Time (Novoe srednevekov'e, 1924; Eng. trans. Donald Attwater, 1933), p. 34
expansion:
Berdyaev (1874–1948) moved from Marxism to Russian Orthodoxy, was expelled by Lenin on the 1922 "philosophers' ship," and spent the rest of his life in Paris. The End of Our Time (in Russian, The New Middle Ages) argues that the Renaissance-humanist project of exalting man without God has exhausted itself and ends in its opposite, the loss of the human person in collectivism and machinery.

His central idea is creativity as the vocation of the human being, developed in The Meaning of the Creative Act (1916). Drawing on Böhme's Ungrund, Berdyaev holds that freedom comes before being, even before God's being, and that the human being is called to co-create, to carry on the creation. Creativity cut off from spirit becomes either titanism or exhaustion. That is the humanist tragedy this passage names.

Berdyaev joins two of your threads that otherwise pull apart: the Romantic-Nietzschean cult of the creator (you liked "every innovator… destroys the existent moral code—in favor of spirit") and a Christian-traditionalist critique of modernity. He keeps both without giving up either.

quote: Love alone is credible; nothing else can be believed, and nothing else ought to be believed. This is the achievement, the “work” of faith: to recognize this absolute prius, which nothing else can surpass; to believe that there is such a thing as love, absolute love, and that there is nothing higher or greater than it; to believe against all the evidence of experience (“credere contra fidem” like “sperare contra spem”), against every “rational” concept of God, which thinks of him in terms of impassibility or, at best, totally pure goodness, but not in terms of this inconceivable and senseless act of love.
author: Hans Urs von Balthasar
work: Love Alone Is Credible (Glaubhaft ist nur Liebe, 1963)
expansion:
Balthasar (1905–1988) was a Swiss theologian and probably the most important Catholic theologian of the twentieth century after Rahner. This short book distills the method of his huge trilogy, which begins with The Glory of the Lord, a theological aesthetics. He rejects the two modern routes to faith. The "cosmological" route makes Christianity fit a metaphysics. The "anthropological" route makes it fit human needs. He proposes a third, the aesthetic: revelation is credible the way a masterpiece is, by showing its own form.

This takes seriously what an unusual number of your liked quotes say: that beauty saves (Dostoevsky), that "the most beautiful is also the most sacred" (Hölderlin), that Christ is "the one figure of absolute beauty." Balthasar argues that when beauty is ignored, goodness loses its pull and truth loses its persuasive force. His summary: "whoever sneers at her name… can no longer pray and soon will no longer be able to love."

Balthasar also offers what you said you wanted when you liked "I don't really do Apologetics anymore." He isn't anti-rational. He thinks that love, seen as glory, is the evidence.

quote: Anxiety increases in direct ratio and proportion as man departs from God. […] There are no plains in the spiritual life; we are either going uphill or coming down. Furthermore the pose of indifference is only intellectual. The will must choose. And even though an "indifferent" soul does not positively reject the infinite, the infinite rejects it.
author: Fulton J. Sheen
work: Peace of Soul (1949), ch. 2, p. 19
expansion:
You liked this line in 2026, and it deserves context. Peace of Soul was Sheen's direct reply to the postwar fashion for psychoanalysis, and in part to Joshua Liebman's bestseller Peace of Mind (1946). Sheen engages Freud more seriously than the title suggests. He accepts that unconscious conflict, repression and anxiety are real. What he disputes is the diagnosis.

His thesis is that modern anxiety is metaphysical, not just psychological. Its root is the frustrated orientation of the finite person toward the infinite, which Augustine called the restless heart and Kierkegaard called Angst before the possibility of freedom. Psychoanalysis can bring a buried guilt to light. Only confession can forgive it. "There are no plains in the spiritual life; we are either going uphill or coming down."

Sheen pairs well with Jung's Modern Man in Search of a Soul — in "Psychotherapists or the Clergy" he wrote that among his patients over thirty-five there was not one whose problem in the last resort was not that of finding a religious outlook on life; he did not say they were healed by it — and with Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety. Read together they work as a three-way debate about faith, psyche and modernity.

quote: Everywhere we remain unfree and chained to technology, whether we passionately affirm or deny it. But we are delivered over to it in the worst possible way when we regard it as something neutral; for this conception of it, to which today we particularly like to do homage, makes us utterly blind to the essence of technology.
author: Martin Heidegger
work: "The Question Concerning Technology" (Die Frage nach der Technik, 1954; trans. William Lovitt, 1977)
expansion:
The lecture was first given in 1949 as part of the Bremen series "Insight into That Which Is." Its well-known argument is that the essence of technology is nothing technological. Technology is a mode of revealing (aletheuein), which Heidegger calls Gestell, enframing. It challenges forth everything, nature and human beings included, as Bestand, standing-reserve, available to be ordered and optimized. The passage chosen here is the opening move: the "instrumental and anthropological" definition of technology as a neutral means is correct but not true, because it hides the fact that we already stand inside a way of disclosing the world.

The genealogy runs from Nietzsche's will to power, which Heidegger read as the completion of metaphysics, through Ernst Jünger's Der Arbeiter (1932), which Heidegger studied closely in seminars. Jünger described the total mobilization of the world by the Gestalt of the worker, and Heidegger recast that as the history of Being. Later readers took the analysis in different directions: Ellul (technique as autonomous), Hans Jonas (an ethics of responsibility), Albert Borgmann (the "device paradigm"), and in the 2020s Byung-Chul Han and Yuk Hui ("cosmotechnics").

Heidegger's remedy isn't rejecting technology. It is Gelassenheit zu den Dingen, releasement toward things, a word he took from Eckhart: say yes and no to technical devices at once, and stay open to the mystery. Following the line Eckhart → Heidegger → today's AI debates ties together your mystical and anti-modern interests in a single argument.

quote: Everything is functioning. This is exactly what is so uncanny, that everything is functioning and that the functioning drives us more and more to even further functioning, and that technology tears men loose from the earth and uproots them. I do not know whether you were frightened, but I at any rate was frightened when I saw pictures coming from the moon to the earth. We don't need any atom bomb. The uprooting of man has already taken place. The only thing we have left is purely technological relationships. This is no longer the earth on which man lives.
author: Martin Heidegger
work: "Only a God Can Save Us" (Der Spiegel interview, recorded 1966, published 1976; trans. M. Alter & J. Caputo)
expansion:
Heidegger gave this interview to Rudolf Augstein and Georg Wolff on condition that it be published only after his death. It was meant to address his 1933 rectorship under the Nazis. It is remembered mostly for its account of the technological situation instead. The passage reacts to the first photographs of the Earth taken from lunar orbit (Lunar Orbiter 1, 1966): what most people saw as a triumph, Heidegger saw as the moment the earth stopped being a dwelling place and became an object seen from nowhere.

"Uprooting" (Entwurzelung) is the key concept. It ties to his 1955 Memorial Address on Gelassenheit, which asks whether "the rootedness, the autochthony of man" can survive the atomic age, and it echoes Weil's L'Enracinement from the other side of the war. Hannah Arendt opens The Human Condition (1958) with a similar response to Sputnik, describing the wish to escape "the earth-bound condition."

Note the tension for your own reading. Heidegger's politics is the shadow cast by his insight, and readers from Levinas to Habermas have said that his nostalgia for rootedness slides easily into nationalism. Weil, writing for the Free French, offers a version of rootedness free of that taint. Reading the two side by side is a good discipline.

quote: There is an exact correspondence between a world where everything seems to be in a state of mere 'becoming', leaving no place for the changeless and the permanent, and the state of mind of men who find all reality in this 'becoming', thus implicitly denying true knowledge as well as the object of that knowledge, namely transcendent and universal principles. […] Matter is essentially multiplicity and division, and this-be it said in passing-is why all that proceeds from matter can beget only strife and all manner of conflicts between peoples as between individuals. The deeper one sinks into matter, the more the elements of division and opposition gain force and scope; and, contrariwise, the more one rises toward pure spirituality, the nearer one approaches that unity
author: René Guénon
work: The Crisis of the Modern World (La Crise du monde moderne, 1927; trans. Marco Pallis, Arthur Osborne & Richard C. Nicholson), pp. 39 and 77–78
expansion:
Guénon (1886–1951) founded the Traditionalist or Perennialist school. He was trained in mathematics, involved in Parisian occultism, then rejected it and converted to Sufism, and he died in Cairo as Shaykh ʿAbd al-Wāḥid Yaḥyā. The Crisis of the Modern World reads modernity as the final phase of the Hindu Kali Yuga, an "anomaly" in which the West alone has cut itself off from metaphysical principles and replaced intellectual intuition with rationalism, contemplation with action, and quality with quantity.

These two passages present the core of his metaphysics of history. The mind that sees only becoming (Bergson, pragmatism, evolutionism) and the world in which everything flows mirror each other, and the descent into matter is a descent into multiplicity and conflict. The account is Neoplatonic (Proclus's procession from the One) joined to the Vedantic doctrine of the cycles. His later Reign of Quantity and the Signs of the Times (1945), which you liked, extends it into a theory of the "solidification" and then the "dissolution" of the modern world.

Guénon influenced Coomaraswamy, Schuon, Evola (whose politicization he largely disowned), Mircea Eliade, and, by contested routes, various contemporary political figures. Mark Sedgwick's Against the Modern World (2004) is the critical history to read next to Guénon's own books. Guénon is worth reading for the rigor of his diagnosis even if his cyclical metaphysics doesn't convince you.

quote: Technology does not fulfill man’s perennial dreams, but craftily mimics them. / Rather than humanizing technology, modern man prefers to technify man. / Modern man calls walking more quickly in the same direction down the same road “change.” The world, in the last three hundred years, has not changed except in that sense.
author: Nicolás Gómez Dávila
work: Escolios a un texto implícito (1977), pp. 12, 123, 227 (trans. Michael Gilleland)
expansion:
Gómez Dávila (1913–1994) was a Colombian who rarely left his library of some 30,000 volumes in Bogotá. He wrote almost entirely in escolios, "glosses" on an "implicit text" he never stated: the Catholic and classical tradition he took to be self-evident. He was nearly unknown until German translations in the 1980s found readers in Ernst Jünger, Botho Strauss and Martin Mosebach. He called himself "a reactionary," which for him meant not nostalgia but refusing the modern faith in progress as the meaning of history.

These three glosses make up a compressed critique of technology. Technology mimics old human dreams instead of fulfilling them: flight without ascent, communication without communion. Modern man "technifies" himself, adapting human nature to the machine. And modern "change" is acceleration along a single track, so that real change, a change of direction, scandalizes. The last gloss anticipates Hartmut Rosa's sociology of acceleration and Han's critique of "the inferno of the same."

The aphorism belongs to a lineage you already like: Pascal, La Rochefoucauld, Joubert, Nietzsche, Kraus, Cioran. Gómez Dávila is its most consistently Catholic modern practitioner. His style suits a quote feed exactly: one sentence that holds an argument.

quote: Faced as we are with this destiny, there is only one world-outlook that is worthy of us, that which has already been mentioned as the Choice of Achilles — better a short life, full of deeds and glory, than a long life without content. Already the danger is so great, for every individual, every class, every people, that to cherish any illusion whatever is deplorable. Time does not suffer itself to be halted; there is no question of prudent retreat or wise renunciation. Only dreamers believe that there is a way out. Optimism is cowardice. We are born into this time and must bravely follow the path to the destined end. There is no other way.
author: Oswald Spengler
work: Man and Technics (Der Mensch und die Technik, 1931; trans. C. F. Atkinson, 1932), §5, pp. 103–104
expansion:
Man and Technics is the short sequel to The Decline of the West (1918–22). Spengler argues that technics is not a set of tools but "the tactics of living," the strategy of a beast of prey. Western or "Faustian" culture has turned it into a will to infinite power over nature. The machine age, on this reading, is a sign of late civilization. It will be "eaten up from within," and our railways and skyscrapers will lie in ruins "like old Memphis and Babylon."

The closing image is the Roman sentry at Pompeii who stayed at his post as the ash fell, "because they forgot to relieve him." It is an ethics of duty without hope. It has Stoic roots (Seneca, Marcus) and Nietzsche's amor fati, and it was taken up as "heroic realism" by the Conservative Revolution: Jünger, Moeller van den Bruck, and in part Heidegger. Note that Spengler rejected the National Socialists, who in turn suppressed his Hour of Decision (1933).

For your reading, the passage is a hard alternative to the Hölderlin and Heidegger line: no saving power grows in the danger, only the dignity of holding one's post. Weigh it against Christian hope (Sheen, Lewis) and against Jünger's later turn from the Worker to the Forest Passage. It's one of the clearest forks in the ideas you've been drawn to.

quote: Whether our modern instance represents a very unusual kind of fear or whether it is simply the return of one and the same cosmic anxiety in the style of the times—we will not pause on this but will rather raise the opposite question, which we think of crucial importance: Might it be possible to lessen the fear even as the automatism progresses or, as can be foreseen, approaches perfection? Would it not be possible to both remain on the ship and retain one’s autonomy of decision—that is, not only to preserve but even to strengthen the roots that are still fixed in the primal ground? This is the real question of our existence.
author: Ernst Jünger
work: The Forest Passage (Der Waldgang, 1951; trans. Thomas Friese, 2013), ch. 13
expansion:
The Forest Passage is the hinge of Jünger's career. The author of Storm of Steel (1920) and The Worker (1932), who had once celebrated total mobilization, offers here a figure of resistance, the Waldgänger, the "forest rebel," borrowed from an old Icelandic legal term for an outlaw who withdrew to the forest. The forest is not a place but an inner condition: "the forest is everywhere," even in the middle of the city, wherever a person keeps his own judgment against automatism and fear.

The metaphor of the ship is central. Leaving the technological ship (the Luddite fantasy, the commune) means drowning. Staying on board as a passive passenger means losing one's freedom. The forest rebel stays on deck and keeps "roots still fixed in the primal ground." The book was written under Allied occupation and in the early Cold War, and it speaks to both totalitarianism and mass democracy. It later influenced the German Greens, the Situationist critique of spectacle, and today's "exit" discourse.

This is the strongest answer in your reading list to the question your likes keep asking: how to live sanely inside a surveillance-heavy, mediated civilization without retreat or capitulation. Pair it with Heidegger's Gelassenheit, written four years later, and with Thoreau, whom Jünger admired.

quote: The numbers of those wanting to abandon ship is growing, among them sharp minds and sound spirits. This would amount to jumping off in mid-ocean. Then hunger, cannibalism, and the sharks arrive—in short, all the terrors of the raft of the Medusa. It is thus under all circumstances advisable to stay on board and on deck, even at the risk of being blown up with everything else.  Ch. 17  This objection is not directed at the poet, who, in his works and in his life, manifests the vast superiority of the world of the muses over the technical world. He helps people find the way back to themselves—the poet is a forest rebel.
author: Ernst Jünger
work: The Forest Passage (Der Waldgang, 1951; trans. Thomas Friese, 2013), ch. 17
expansion:
This continues the image of the ship and turns to who the forest rebel's allies are. Jünger names the poet first, because the poet "manifests the vast superiority of the world of the muses over the technical world." That echoes Hölderlin's "what remains is founded by the poets" and anticipates Heidegger's thesis that only poetry and thought, "a might without force," can answer uprooting.

Jünger's warning against "jumping off in mid-ocean" is aimed at a specific postwar temptation: fleeing to America or to a commune, or refusing modernity altogether. The raft of the Medusa refers to Géricault's painting of shipwrecked men driven to cannibalism, his image of what anarchic exodus becomes. His position is close to Goethe's "renunciation" and to Gómez Dávila's: you stay inside the world while keeping a sovereign inner distance.

Since you like art (Shishkin, Sohlberg) and poetry (Emerson, Keats, Rilke), this gives your aesthetic interests a role in public life. In Jünger's sense beauty is not escapism. It is a form of resistance.

quote: No technique is possible when men are free. … Technique requires predictability and, no less, exactness of prediction. It is necessary, then, that technique prevail over the human being. … The individual must be fashioned by techniques …
author: Jacques Ellul
work: The Technological Society (La Technique ou l'enjeu du siècle, 1954; trans. John Wilkinson, 1964), p. 138
expansion:
Ellul (1912–1994) was a French Protestant sociologist and lay theologian, a Resistance member, and a Righteous Among the Nations. Aldous Huxley brought The Technological Society to an American publisher. Ellul's subject is la technique: not machines, but "the totality of methods rationally arrived at and having absolute efficiency" in every field, economics, administration, propaganda and psychology included. Technique is autonomous, self-augmenting, universal, and, as this passage says, incompatible with human freedom understood as unpredictability.

Ellul's analysis runs parallel to Heidegger's but is sociological and empirical rather than ontological, and his Christian dialectic (developed in The Ethics of Freedom and The Meaning of the City) keeps it from fatalism. Freedom is the work of grace and of resistance, not a natural condition. His Propaganda (1962) argued that modern people want propaganda because it relieves them of having to judge for themselves. That deserves a look given the media-distrust theme in your 2020 likes.

Ellul is the systematic link between your old political skepticism and your new spiritual interests. His followers include Ivan Illich, Neil Postman, and, in passing, the Kaczynski manifesto (whose tranquility line you liked), a lineage Ellul himself would have rejected.

quote: The right hemisphere underwrites breadth and flexibility of attention, where the left hemisphere brings to bear focussed attention. This has the related consequence that the right hemisphere sees things whole, and in their context, where the left hemisphere sees things abstracted from context, and broken into parts, from which it then reconstructs a 'whole': something very different.
author: Iain McGilchrist
work: The Master and His Emissary: The Divided Brain and the Making of the Western World (Yale, 2009), ch. 1, p. 27
expansion:
McGilchrist is a psychiatrist and former Oxford literary scholar. His argument is that the two hemispheres differ not in what they do (language versus images, the pop myth) but in how they attend. The left grasps, isolates, categorizes and manipulates. The right is open to the living, the implicit, the embodied and the unique. The title's parable: the right hemisphere is the master, the left its emissary, and in Western history the emissary has usurped the master.

Part II of the book reads Western cultural history as swings between the two modes: the Greek balance, Roman bureaucracy, the Renaissance, the Reformation's iconoclasm, Enlightenment rationalism, the Romantic protest, and modernism's fragmentation. It draws explicitly on Goethe, Scheler, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty and Whitehead. The sequel, The Matter with Things (2021), becomes an explicit metaphysics close to Neoplatonism and process thought.

McGilchrist gives a neuroscientific vocabulary for what Goethe (delicate empiricism), Pieper (intellectus versus ratio), Weil (attention), Keats (Negative Capability) and Pascal (the heart) each described. His reception is mixed: critics question how well the clinical evidence carries the cultural argument. It is still one of the most ambitious syntheses of your interests by a living writer.

quote: Twenty-first-century society is no longer a disciplinary society, but rather an achievement society [Leistungsgesellschaft]. Disciplinary society is still governed by no. Its negativity produces madmen and criminals. In contrast, achievement society creates depressives and losers. […] However, the disappearance of domination does not entail freedom. Instead, it makes freedom and constraint coincide. Thus, the achievement-subject gives itself over to compulsive freedom--that is, to the free constraint of maximizing achievement. Excess work and performance escalate into auto-exploitation.
author: Byung-Chul Han
work: The Burnout Society (Müdigkeitsgesellschaft, 2010; trans. Erik Butler, Stanford 2015), pp. 8–11
expansion:
Han, a Korean-born philosopher trained in Heidegger studies in Freiburg and teaching in Berlin, updates Foucault. Foucault's "disciplinary society" ran on prohibition and the word no, and produced madmen and criminals. Today's "achievement society" runs on the unlimited "Yes, we can" and produces depression, ADHD and burnout. Domination doesn't vanish. It becomes internal: the achievement-subject exploits himself and experiences it as freedom.

The analysis draws on Hegel's master-slave dialectic (the master and slave now in one person), Nietzsche's "last man," and Heidegger's critique of the will. Han's remedy is a recovery of "profound boredom," contemplative lingering (Verweilen), and the vita contemplativa, which places him next to Pieper on leisure and Picard on silence. A short book, Vita Contemplativa (2022), makes the connection explicit.

Your old likes on hustle and wealth (Naval, leverage) and your new likes on contemplation (Weil, Eckhart) meet at Han's diagnosis. He explains why the optimized life feels like captivity, and he names the kind of freedom your recent reading points to.

quote: Originally I was not possessed by gloomy thoughts. My concern, what confronted me with my real problem, was beauty alone. But I do not think that the war affected me by filling my mind with gloomy thoughts. When people concentrate on the idea of beauty, they are, without realizing it, confronted with the darkest thoughts that exist in this world. That, I suppose, is how human beings are made.
author: Yukio Mishima
work: The Temple of the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji, 1956; trans. Ivan Morris, 1959), ch. 2
expansion:
The novel is a fictionalized account of the 1950 arson of Kyoto's Kinkaku-ji by a young acolyte. Its narrator, Mizoguchi, a stutterer, becomes obsessed with the temple's beauty as something absolute, unreachable and finally intolerable: beauty that stands between him and life. The passage states the novel's metaphysics. Contemplating beauty leads not to serenity but to the darkest thoughts.

Mishima writes against the Platonic-Christian identification of beauty and goodness you meet in Plotinus, Dostoevsky and Balthasar, and in favor of a darker line. Its sources include the Buddhist doctrine of impermanence (mono no aware), the Zen koan of Nansen killing the cat (central to the novel), Baudelaire, and Rilke's "beauty is nothing but the beginning of terror." For Mishima beauty is tied to death. His own life ended in ritual suicide in 1970, and his Sun and Steel (1968) shows how he tied together aesthetics, the body and masculinity.

You liked Kyoto, Japanese aesthetics and physical discipline, so Mishima is a natural point of contact, and the necessary counterpoint to your Platonic and Christian aesthetics. He forces the question of whether beauty saves or destroys. Dostoevsky's own answer, through Dmitri Karamazov, was that "beauty is a terrible and awful thing… here God and the devil are fighting."
